sections.h2: How an Iowa tax sale works
sections.html:
Iowa counties sell delinquent property taxes at an annual public sale, and the buyer receives a certificate, not a deed. On the third Monday in June, the county treasurer offers every parcel with delinquent taxes, though the treasurer may pick a different June date for good cause (Iowa Code 446.7).

The deed comes much later, and only if the owner and other interested parties fail to redeem in time. That gap gives a homeowner room to act. It is also why buying a certificate is not the same as owning the house.

Parcels held by a county or city, or owned by the state or a political subdivision, cannot be sold, and a sale of them is void.

sections.h2: Timeline leading up to the June sale
sections.html:
Taxes first go late, then the owner gets notices, then the parcel is listed for sale.

WhenWhat happens
September 1First-half installment due, payable through September 30
OctoberUnpaid first half becomes delinquent and begins to accrue interest
March 1Second-half installment due, payable through March 31
AprilUnpaid second half becomes delinquent
By May 1Owner notice of the coming sale mailed first class (section 446.9)
One to three weeks before saleNotice published in an official county newspaper (section 446.9)
Third Monday in JuneAnnual tax sale

Late interest on delinquent installments is 1.5 percent per month. The Iowa treasurers' important dates page has the statewide calendar. A mortgagee or other interested party can ask for its own notice by filing a request one month before the sale with a $25 fee per parcel, valid five years.

sections.h2: Who can bid, and what the winner gets
sections.html:
Bidders compete on percentage, and the lowest percentage wins. Bids must be at least one percent, and ties are settled by random selection (section 446.16). Bidders need a federal tax identification number and either a registered agent or a verified statement on file, and the treasurer may charge a reasonable registration fee.

If no one bids, or the bid falls below the total due, the county bids the total amount due and no cash changes hands (section 446.19). Parcels left unsold for want of bidders can be offered again, and a county holding such a public bidder certificate may accept redemption any time before the deed issues.

The certificate holder pays later-year taxes and adds them to the amount the owner must redeem. The holder owns a claim to the parcel, not the parcel.

Redemption costs the sale amount, the certificate fee and later-year amounts, plus interest of 2 percent per month. Each fraction of a month counts as a full month (section 447.1). Interest has a $1 minimum, and payment must reach the treasurer by the last day of the month to avoid another month of interest.

  • Costs of serving the redemption notice, certified mail, any publication and the record search are added to the amount (section 447.13).
  • If the holder is not a county, an Iowa title guaranty abstractor or an attorney admitted in Iowa must do the record search, and the search charge is capped at $300.
  • Costs must be filed with the treasurer before redemption is complete, or the treasurer cannot collect them.

Interest runs from the sale, so a delay of even a few weeks can add another full month. Your own county treasurer can quote the exact payoff. The Linn County Treasurer, for example, processes redemptions and takes calls at 319-892-5500 about the fee and documents.

sections.h2: How long the right to redeem lasts
sections.html:
The right to redeem lasts at least until ninety days after the redemption notice is completely served. A certificate holder may serve that notice one year and nine months after the sale (section 447.9). Earlier notice is possible on some sales:

  • Regular annual sale: one year and nine months after the sale.
  • Public bidder sale (446.18): nine months after the sale.
  • Abandoned residential or vacant lot (446.19A) and public nuisance (446.19B) sales: three months after the sale.

The notice goes by regular and certified mail to the owner and the occupant, and to mortgagees and other record interest holders. If service cannot be made that way, the holder publishes it once in an official county newspaper. Service is complete only when an affidavit is filed with the treasurer, and the ninety days then begin to run (section 447.12).

The deadline is close of business on day 90, or the next business day if day 90 falls on a weekend or holiday. A postmark does not count, so the payment itself must be received.

sections.h2: Protections for owners who cannot pay
sections.html:
A few narrow ones exist. A county board of supervisors can redeem an owner-occupied residential parcel for an owner unable to contribute to public revenue, on petition (section 447.9(3)). A legal representative can redeem for a person with a legal disability before the deed is delivered. After delivery, that person has to bring an equitable action within one year after the disability is removed (section 447.7).

Notice also protects owners. If an owner of record was not served the redemption notice under section 447.9, the tax deed is void, subject to the affidavit rules in sections 448.15 and 448.16 (section 448.3).

These routes are limited. They are no substitute for paying the taxes or selling the home while the redemption right is still open.

sections.h2: What an Iowa tax deed does
sections.html:
The county treasurer issues the deed after the ninety-day period, and it vests the state's, the county's and the former owner's interest in the purchaser (sections 448.1 and 448.3). The treasurer records the deed before handing it over and receives $25 per deed.

A deed can be attacked only through an equitable action in district court, and the challenger must prove one of four things: the parcel was not subject to tax, the taxes were paid before the sale, the parcel was redeemed, or there was an entire omission in listing, assessment, levy, notice or sale (section 448.6). Such actions must be brought within three years after the deed is executed and recorded (section 448.12).

A deed holder in possession may also file an affidavit with the county recorder. Other claimants then have 120 days to file a claim and 60 more days to sue. If no claim is filed, the title is conclusively established (sections 448.15 and 448.16).

Someone who stays in possession after a valid tax deed faces forcible entry and detainer (section 648.1).

sections.h2: Selling before the tax deed issues
sections.html:
In most cases you can, because the owner keeps title until a deed is delivered. A sale that pays the redemption amount at closing ends the tax sale and clears that debt from the title.

Three steps help. Ask the county treasurer for a current redemption figure and the date interest next rolls over. Find out whether a redemption notice has been served, since that starts the ninety-day clock. Then line up a buyer who can close before the clock runs out. Cash Home Buyers buys Iowa houses as-is and can move on a short timeline when the facts allow it. We make no promise on price before reviewing the property.

At closing, the title company pays the treasurer from your proceeds, gets a receipt, and the certificate holder is paid through the county. Bring your tax bills, any notice you received in the mail, and the parcel number to the first conversation.

faqs.q: When is the Iowa tax sale held?
faqs.a: The third Monday in June, unless the county treasurer sets a different June date for good cause.

faqs.q: What interest rate applies to Iowa tax sale redemption?
faqs.a: Two percent per month, and any fraction of a month counts as a full month. Costs and later-year taxes are added.

faqs.q: How long do I have to redeem after the redemption notice?
faqs.a: Ninety days after service of the notice is complete. Payment must be received by close of business on day 90 or the next business day, and a postmark does not count.

faqs.q: Who issues an Iowa tax deed?
faqs.a: The county treasurer, after the ninety-day period, once the purchaser returns the certificate and pays the deed and recording fees.

faqs.q: Can an Iowa tax deed be challenged?
faqs.a: Yes, but only in an equitable action in district court on narrow grounds, brought within three years of the deed being executed and recorded.
